title: The impact of generative AI on academic reading and writing: a synthesis of recent evidence (2023–2025)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly growing literature on generative AI (GAI) in higher education, with a specific focus on reading and writing practices in the social sciences. The authors ask what the recent evidence (2023–2025) shows about how GAI tools, especially ChatGPT and related applications, are being used, what benefits and risks are reported, and which theoretical and methodological trends characterize this emerging field.

The review used a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review and the SALSA framework to search Scopus and Web of Science for open-access English- and Spanish-language journal articles published between January 1, 2023 and March 7, 2025. The final corpus included 136 studies, most of which involved university students, though some also included educators. The reviewed studies covered a wide range of contexts across multiple countries, with especially strong representation from Asia, Europe, and North America.

Overall, the review concludes that GAI is widely perceived as useful for supporting academic writing, idea generation, translation, grammar correction, paraphrasing, and formative feedback. The strongest reported benefits are improvements in text quality, especially coherence, discursive organization, lexical richness, and argumentation, as well as greater student autonomy in self-editing. At the same time, the review highlights important concerns: overreliance on AI, reduced metacognitive engagement, plagiarism and authorship issues, weak detection reliability, bias, and inequitable access. The paper argues that responsible integration depends on critical AI literacy, teacher guidance, transparent use, and redesigned assessment practices.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/model family used for text generation, dialogue, and writing assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the most frequently referenced GAI tool in the reviewed literature, used for academic reading/writing support, idea generation, paraphrasing, and formative feedback in higher education. The review also discusses its use in comparison with peer and teacher feedback and in reading comprehension tasks.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was repeatedly associated with improved text quality in academic writing, especially coherence, discursive organization, lexical richness, and argumentation. The review also reports benefits for narrative fluency, originality, idea generation, paraphrasing, and self-editing autonomy, but notes risks of overreliance and reduced metacognitive engagement.
findings.measure: Text quality; coherence; discursive organization; lexical richness; argumentation; narrative fluency; originality; paraphrasing; self-editing autonomy
findings.sample_size: n=136 (review corpus); underlying study sample sizes not consistently reported

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that ChatGPT-supported formative feedback improved English-as-a-second-language writing skills compared with traditional methods. It also notes that students and teachers often valued ChatGPT feedback as practical, interactive, and adaptive, although responses could be inconsistent and required teacher supervision.
findings.measure: Formative feedback quality; writing skill improvement compared with traditional methods; perceived usefulness of feedback

findings.finding_summary: For reading-related tasks, the review notes a study on reading comprehension and inference using AI-based short-answer grading, and cites findings that students had lower comprehension than ChatGPT in one context. However, the paper does not provide pooled effect sizes or a K-12-specific estimate, and the evidence is not directly about school-age learners.

identified_tools.name: Grammarly
identified_tools.description: An AI-assisted writing and grammar correction tool that provides feedback on language accuracy, style, and text quality.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed in the review as a commonly studied AI writing support tool and in at least one quasi-experimental study of writing improvement.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that Grammarly had a positive impact on grammatical accuracy and lexical richness in writing in a quasi-experimental study. The paper presents this as evidence that AI writing support can improve surface-level writing quality.

identified_tools.name: QuillBot
identified_tools.description: An AI paraphrasing and writing-support tool used for rewriting, paraphrasing, and text improvement.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned as one of the AI tools adopted in writing classrooms and as a tool for improving paraphrasing skills.

findings.finding_summary: The review states that QuillBot was used to improve paraphrasing skills and that adoption of QuillBot alongside other tools was associated with improvements in content and organization of texts. No pooled effect size or study-level estimate is provided.
findings.measure: Paraphrasing skills; content and organization of texts

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, not a direct experimental study, so the evidence is synthesized rather than primary causal evidence. The included literature is methodologically mixed and heavily based on surveys and quasi-experiments, which limits certainty for outcome effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The review reports positive associations for writing quality, feedback, and paraphrasing, but no pooled effect sizes or K-12-specific direct estimates are given. The impact appears promising but is mostly modest/unclear because the evidence is indirect and primarily higher-education focused.
